Preparation for Sampling Each sampling method and recruitment strategy has specific operational requirements, but the following considerations are generally applicable: Set clear expectations with gatekeepers regarding survey activities, including the requirements for listing individuals at the location, the physical space needed for interviews, specimen collection, or providing test results, the time required for each interview, and any testing procedures. Identify a private area suitable for conducting interviews and collecting biological specimens. Train survey staff on participant protections, ensuring participants understand and sign confidentiality agreements. Schedule participant sampling or interviews. Investigators must adhere to the survey protocol and activity flow chart. Depending on the location, data and specimen collection may occur in the field, requiring staff to carry necessary equipment such as backpacks, cooler boxes, flashlights, clipboards, and tablets. If feasible, a van or bus can enhance mobility, facilitate data collection, and improve security and privacy. Staff should also have access to essential items like cash, condoms, lubricants, and clean injection kits. Monitoring Survey Progress Adherence to standard operating procedures (SOPs) is critical for both probability and non-probability sampling surveys. Survey progress and sample composition must be documented to assess biases and data quality. SOPs should be developed, and any changes must be recorded. During sampling, staff should document the number of individuals screened for eligibility, those eligible, those who consent, and reasons for refusal. They should also track the number of participants agreeing to specimen collection, those receiving results, and reasons for refusal. If vouchers or coupons are used, their issuance and redemption should be monitored. Attention to data and specimen quality is essential, and potential non-sampling errors, such as reporting bias or testing quality issues, should be noted. Survey Implementation and Quality Assurance This section provides guidance on using conventional cluster sampling (CCS). It includes preparations for participant sampling, confidentiality procedures, field staff setup, and methods for sampling individuals from a list. In CCS, the target population is associated with fixed clusters, meaning individuals can reliably be found at the same cluster location. A complete list of individuals associated with a cluster should be obtained or created. Examples of appropriate CCS applications include brothel-based sex workers, detainees in prisons, military personnel in barracks, and people who inject drugs (PWID) in treatment facilities. Steps for Sampling Preparation During the survey planning phase, after selecting cluster locations, the following steps should be taken: Contact gatekeepers at each cluster location and explain the survey objectives. Visit each cluster location to build rapport, understand potential field issues, answer questions, and address concerns. Observe the physical layout of the location and work with the gatekeeper to identify a private area for interviews and specimen collection. Discuss confidentiality with key individuals in the selected clusters. Set expectations for survey activities with the gatekeeper, including requirements for listing individuals, physical space, time needed for interviews, and testing procedures. Request a complete list of eligible individuals connected to the cluster location, stratified by criteria such as gender or age group, if necessary. Schedule participant sampling dates. Special Confidentiality Considerations Gatekeepers do not have the right to access information collected from survey participants. Lists of eligible individuals should be specific enough to identify individuals but must be destroyed after all selected individuals have been approached. If a gatekeeper insists on accessing survey data, the cluster location should be excluded from the survey. Survey Implementation Using Time-Location Sampling (TLS) TLS is used to survey populations that move freely through physical venues but may not visit them regularly. Investigators create a sampling frame of all possible venues and times the target population may visit. Sampling is conducted from a list of venue-day-time combinations to obtain a representative sample. Survey staff then visit the venues to collect data during sampling events. TLS is suitable for populations such as sex workers at bars or hotels, men who have sex with men (MSM) or transgender individuals at clubs, and PWID at drug-related venues. Recruitment and Data Collection Survey staff should include supervisors, counters, recruiters, interviewers, counselors, and laboratory technicians. Recruitment areas should also provide privacy for interviews and testing. Steps for Data Collection 1. Meet with Gatekeepers: Explain the survey's goals, emphasizing confidentiality and minimal interference with venue operations. 2. Prepare Materials: 3. Set Up Recruitment and Testing Areas: 4. Screen for Eligibility: Use standardized tools to confirm participant eligibility and document the process. 5. Obtain Informed Consent: Follow SOPs to document consent outcomes. 6. Conduct Interviews: Administer face-to-face or self-administered interviews using electronic questionnaires. 7. Provide Counseling and Testing: Escort participants to designated areas for counseling, specimen collection, and testing. Record test results and provide them to participants as appropriate. 8. Offer Referrals: Refer newly diagnosed HIV-positive individuals or those not in care to medical services. Provide information on future testing locations for HIV-negative individuals and referrals for other health or social services as needed. 9. Provide STI Treatment: If part of the protocol, offer treatment for treatable sexually transmitted infections (STIs). 10. Provide Compensation: If included in the protocol, compensate participants appropriately. Debriefing and Field Notes At the end of data collection at a cluster location, conduct a debriefing with field staff to discuss issues or problems encountered. Document any challenges, barriers, or recruitment statistics to adjust future field operations. Supervisors should notify investigators if SOPs or protocols require amendments.
